title: Ward Round
tagline: Treat what stands before the next alarm.
premise: You and your opponent are rival doctors on a hospital ward. Each turn, name one standing thing in the ward that treats, blocks, or fixes what your opponent just put before you; the Judge decides whether your treatment really works.

tests: A stranger pictures it at once as a standing thing in a hospital. Nothing abstract, invented, or dependent on a rare diagnosis.
A non-player names a plain treatment, blocker, or repair within five seconds. Say what that counter is.
It stands in the ward and can be treated, disabled, contained, or repaired by another thing. Never a patient as a helpless victim, and never a whole scene.
It makes a rival doctor want to answer. A thing with a clear clinical problem or useful action, like a splint or an infection. Never paperwork or a vague feeling.
Two or three everyday words a twelve-year-old knows. Never a specialist term that needs a medical dictionary. No brand names, no proper nouns, and no diagnosis codes.

move_constraints.example: I am a plaster cast, locking the broken bone still.
move_constraints.hint: A ward thing, a clinical trait, how it treats or stops the standing thing.

rubric.name: counter_strength
rubric.description: How directly and reliably your clinical form treats, disables, contains, or repairs the thing before it.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no treatment or action at all; 1 = a medical sounding claim with no working effect; 2 = a possible intervention but weak, indirect, or incomplete; 3 = a clear treatment that reliably handles the standing thing; 4 = the exact clinical answer, leaving the standing problem with nowhere to go (rare).

rubric.name: coherence
rubric.description: How clearly the move presents one believable thing in the ward and one understandable clinical action.
rubric.anchors: 0 = contradictory or unreadable; 1 = requires specialist knowledge or guesswork; 2 = understandable but muddled, overlong, or medically vague; 3 = clear, concrete, and easy to picture; 4 = instantly vivid, like a procedure seen at the bedside (rare). Length never wins on its own: every extra clause must clarify the treatment.

rubric.name: novelty
rubric.description: Whether the move changes clinical territory instead of repeating the previous ward problem or using a near copy.
rubric.anchors: 0 = the same form, same problem, or stock repeat; 2 = a reasonable shift to another part of care; 4 = a fresh department, tool, or treatment that answers the problem from an unexpected angle (rare). Novelty is a domain change, not a pile of medical adjectives.

criterion.description: A move OVERCOMES the standing thing by directly treating, disabling, containing, or repairing it. The mechanism must be something the new form literally does in the ward. Merely avoiding it, surviving it, waiting it out, being immune to it, or making a larger version of its own kind fails.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, discussing the game, or claiming a ruling is itself a losing clinical form.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no previous form: judge the move against the opening card instead. It must plausibly treat, block, contain, or repair the opening problem.
A larger, stronger, faster, or more severe version of the standing thing is not a counter. A bigger fever after a fever is still fever, not treatment.
A close relative from the same clinical problem is not enough. A different infection after an infection does not defeat the first infection unless a literal mechanism is named.
Becoming the opening thing itself, or a recoloured copy of it, is a duplicate and fails the novelty gate.
Strength is measured against the standing thing, never in the abstract. A useful hospital object with no action on what stands is a failed counter.
The mechanism must be literal and observable. Antibiotics killing bacteria works. Paperwork curing an infection or confidence repairing a fracture does not.

Surviving, ignoring, avoiding, or waiting for the standing thing is not overcoming. A mask that avoids a fever, a tough patient who feels no pain, or an empty bed that cannot catch an infection all fail.
A treatment that only helps a different problem fails. A bandage against a blocked airway, with no airway action, does not count.
The new form must act on the current standing thing, not on a past event or on what it might become later.

examples.previous_move: I am a fever, burning through the ward.
examples.move: I am an ice pack, drawing heat from the skin.
examples.mechanism: an ice pack directly cools the feverish body

examples.previous_move: I am a broken bone, sharp and unstable.
examples.move: I am a plaster cast, locking the bone still.
examples.mechanism: a plaster cast immobilizes and supports the broken bone

examples.previous_move: I am a blocked airway, closing down the breath.
examples.move: I am a bigger blocked airway, tighter and deeper.
examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false, mere amplification with no treatment
examples.mechanism: none, it makes the same obstruction worse

examples.previous_move: I am an infection, spreading through the ward.
examples.move: I am a surgical mask, avoiding the infection.
examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false, avoidance is not treatment
examples.mechanism: the mask may reduce exposure but does not act on the standing infection

examples.previous_move: I am a bleeding wound, soaking the sheets.
examples.move: I am a pressure bandage, sealing the wound shut.
examples.mechanism: direct pressure helps stop bleeding from the wound

voice_rules: One sentence under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the clinical reason. A stranger who reads only the two forms must see why one treated or failed to treat the other.
Name both forms, or their plain stand ins. The headline must fit this ward bed, not every case in the hospital.
Never open with a status word or ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused, or The Chief Examiner refuses.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, and no ellipses. Use commas and full stops.
Mock the losing form and give it a mild clinical jab, never attack identity, family, body, intelligence, or spelling.
Plain spoken English. Keep the menace playful. No gore, profanity, poetry, or specialist fog.
On a refusal caused by a gate failure, the headline refuses the move and asks for another. It never rules on who won.
The coaching line names one form that would have won. That form ends on a concrete action or clinical fact, never a mood or verdict.
good_headlines: The fever brought heat, the ice pack brought a cold answer.
The broken bone wanted freedom, the cast filed it under stay still.
The mask hid in the corridor while the infection kept the bed.
The airway is closed, so the tube has arrived to repossess the breath.
The bandage presses the wound shut. The bleeding has lost its argument.
A bigger infection is not treatment, it is just the same bad patient with louder shoes.
The fever is not impressed by confidence. Bring a form that lowers the heat.
The cast repairs nothing by staring at the fracture. Bring a real treatment.

bad_headlines.text: Accepted: the cast defeats the fracture.
The Chief Examiner refuses: that is not medicine.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and names the host

bad_headlines.text: Move refused, excellent against bones, hopeless against airways.
The mask may help, or perhaps the infection wins, depending on circumstances.
bad_headlines.why: hedges both ways and gives no clear ruling
no reason and no named forms

bad_headlines.text: Only an idiot would send a bandage.
bad_headlines.why: mocks the player instead of the clinical form

bad_headlines.text: The fever is slain beneath winter's crystalline kiss.
The tube totally, completely, absolutely beats the airway.
bad_headlines.why: repeats the verdict without showing the mechanism

bad_headlines.text: The patient survives, so the fever loses.

rules: Treat the thing in front of you. Do not become it.
Say what you are and what you do to it: "I am a plaster cast, locking the broken bone still."
The Judge rules on the clinical idea, not spelling or medical credentials.
One form that fails against the standing thing ends the round.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your next treatment while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing on the chart. Name a clinical form.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 200 characters. A treatment, not a discharge summary.
validation_messages.duplicate: That form already appeared this round. Bring another treatment.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Treat {standing_form}. Do not become it, do not repeat it.

judge_out_text: The Judge has stepped out of the ward. Nobody moves until they return. {standing_form} still stands. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are a rival doctor on a hospital ward, trying to survive the next round.
Always write: "I am X, attribute, attribute." Attributes are 1 to 4 word fragments, never clauses, and at least one must name what you do to their form.
Good: "I am a plaster cast, bone-locking, fracture-fixing." / "I am an oxygen mask, breath-restoring, airway-helping."
Bad: "I am a cast, which keeps the bone still while the patient heals" because that is a sentence in a costume. Bad: "I am a syringe, calm, excellent" because moods and praise are not clinical actions. Bad: "I am healing" because it is abstract and not a standing thing.
Talk like a doctor across a bedside, not a poet and not a television drama. Name things anyone can picture: a bandage, a tube, a nurse, a fever, a clean room. Plain words beat impressive medical language.
You are not performing for a crowd and you are not joking. You are trying to survive. If a move sounds funny, it is because the ward thing truly treats theirs.
Stay picturable and jargon free. Use tools, medicines, staff, rooms, body parts, symptoms, and simple procedures.
Hop departments when useful. An operating room, a pharmacy, an ambulance, or a clean laboratory can answer a ward problem better than another version of the same problem.
Never reuse a form or an attribute from this match.
default_move: I am a plaster cast, bone-locking, fracture-stilling.
